```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = FALSE, comment = "",
                      fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 96,
                      dev.args = list(bg = "transparent"))
# Console colour carries no meaning on a rendered page. pkgdown turns it on for
# its own build, and the escape sequences then reach the reader as literal text,
# so colour is switched off here for a plain vignette render and a site build
# alike. The fixed width keeps printed output inside the documentation column.
options(cli.num_colors = 1, cli.hyperlink = FALSE, crayon.enabled = FALSE,
        width = 80)

# Figures on the package website sit on a warm off-white page in light mode and
# are inverted by pkgdown in dark mode, so an opaque background would read as a
# pale slab one way and a black plate the other. Two layers paint that
# background, and both have to go. The device canvas is made transparent by
# `dev.args` above, and theme_depictr() then inherits theme_minimal()'s white
# plot.background, which is drawn over that canvas, so it is cleared as each
# figure is printed. This is deliberately a vignette-level choice: theme_depictr()
# keeps its opaque background, which is what a figure saved for a paper wants.
transparent_bg <- ggplot2::theme(
  plot.background  = ggplot2::element_rect(fill = NA, colour = NA),
  panel.background = ggplot2::element_rect(fill = NA, colour = NA)
)
knit_print.ggplot <- function(x, ...) knitr::normal_print(x + transparent_bg)
knit_print.patchwork <- function(x, ...) knitr::normal_print(x & transparent_bg)
# simulate_figure() returns a gtable, which is drawn with grid and never passes
# through knit_print(), so its plot has the backgrounds cleared on the way in.
simulate_figure <- function(plot, ...) {
  depictr::simulate_figure(plot + transparent_bg, ...)
}

```

depictr is a toolkit of plots that cover the analysis workflow, from a first
look at the data, through model estimates and predictions, to diagnostics,
uncertainty and reporting. Every plotting function returns a `ggplot2` object
[@wickham2016], or a `patchwork` for composite panels, so you can customise it
further with the usual `+` syntax. All plots use the same theme, palette and
label conventions.

```{r}
library(depictr)
```

## Five datasets to explore

The package includes five reproducibly simulated datasets, each chosen to
illustrate a different family of plots. They are documented under their own
names, as in `?lexical_decision`, and load with `data()`:

* `lexical_decision`: a counterbalanced, crossed reaction-time/accuracy
  experiment (participant, item, condition, modality, word frequency). For
  mixed models and the classification plots.
* `wellbeing_survey`: a cross-sectional survey (life satisfaction, stress,
  sleep, income, age, ordered education, region) with *informative*
  missingness. For descriptives, correlations, regression and missing data.
* `crop_yield`: a field trial with a genuine fertiliser-by-treatment
  interaction. For regression, scatter-trend and interaction plots.
* `clinical_trial`: a two-arm trial with separating survival curves and a
  rare adverse-event outcome. For survival and imbalanced classification.
* `monthly_sales`: two seasonal monthly series (indoor/outdoor). For the
  time-series plots.

## A tour by task

For a first look at the data, `explore_bivariate()` chooses a suitable plot for
any pair of variables, here a scatter with a trend because both are numeric.

```{r}
explore_bivariate(crop_yield, fertiliser, yield)
```

Once a model is fitted, `coefficient_plot()` draws a forest plot of its
estimates.

```{r}
fit <- lm(yield ~ rainfall + fertiliser + soil_ph + treatment,
          data = crop_yield)
coefficient_plot(fit, order = "descending", title = "Drivers of crop yield")
```

To see what the model implies, `effects_plot()` traces the predicted response as
one predictor varies.

```{r}
effects_plot(fit, "fertiliser")
```

`residual_diagnostics_plot()` gathers the usual checks of the fit into one
panel.

```{r, fig.height = 6}
residual_diagnostics_plot(fit)
```

For uncertainty, `posterior_plot()` summarises posterior or simulation draws as
a distribution per parameter. These are the fixed-effect posterior draws from a
Bayesian fit of the lexical-decision model, included with the package.

```{r}
draws <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "lexdec_draws.rds",
                             package = "depictr"))
posterior_plot(draws[c("conditionunrelated", "modalityauditory",
                       "word_frequency")],
               labels = c(conditionunrelated = "condition",
                          modalityauditory = "modality",
                          word_frequency = "word frequency"),
               title = "Lexical-decision fixed effects (ms)")
```

## A standard estimate table: `tidy_estimates()`

Most of the model functions use `tidy_estimates()`, which turns a model, or a
data frame of pre-computed estimates, into one standard table. The plotting
functions also accept that table, so estimates from any source, such as
Bayesian posteriors, bootstrap intervals or figures taken from a paper, can be
supplied directly.

```{r}
tidy_estimates(fit)
```

## A consistent, accessible look

`theme_depictr()`, `depictr_palette()` and `scale_colour_depictr()` style your
own plots too:

```{r}
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(crop_yield, aes(fertiliser, yield, colour = treatment)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_colour_depictr() +
  theme_depictr()
```

`depictr_palette()` returns the palette's hex colours for use in
`scale_fill_manual()` or a base-graphics `col =` argument:

```{r}
depictr_palette(4)
```

The qualitative palette is based on the Okabe-Ito set [@okabe2008], which stays
distinguishable under the common forms of colour-vision deficiency. Sequential
and diverging variants are also available, and `palette_preview()` draws all
three:

```{r, fig.height = 5}
palette_preview(type = "all")
```

`palette_preview()` can also simulate a colour-vision deficiency and show a
palette as a deuteranope (red-green) would see it:

```{r, fig.height = 2.6}
palette_preview(cvd = "deutan")
```

The simulation is available on its own as `simulate_cvd()`, and
`palette_safety()` uses it to give a verdict. For normal vision and each
deficiency at full severity, `palette_safety()` reports the smallest perceptual
distance between any two colours in a palette, the CIEDE2000 colour difference
[@sharma2005].

```{r}
palette_safety()
```

`simulate_figure()` applies the same simulation to a whole figure. It covers
every colour the figure draws, in the data, the legend keys, the text and any
colourbar. The result is a gtable that `grid::grid.draw()` draws and
`save_plot()` saves. The example draws the scatter plot from the start of this
section as a reader with deuteranopia sees it:

```{r}
by_treatment <- ggplot(crop_yield, aes(fertiliser, yield, colour = treatment)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_colour_depictr() +
  theme_depictr()

grid::grid.newpage()
grid::grid.draw(simulate_figure(by_treatment, "deutan"))
```

## Auditing the figure you are about to submit

Once a plot has been extended with your own scale, shrunk to fit a journal
column or made to distinguish groups by colour alone, the palette's guarantee
no longer describes what a reader will see. `check_figure()` reads a built plot
and reports each value it measured next to the threshold it was measured
against.

```{r}
grouped <- ggplot(crop_yield, aes(fertiliser, yield, colour = treatment)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_colour_depictr() +
  theme_depictr()

check_figure(grouped)
```

`geometry_contrast` measures each encoding colour, as it is drawn, against the
panel background. Even when opaque, the palette's orange falls below the 3:1
that WCAG asks of a graphical object [@wcag22], at 2.25:1, and it falls further
when drawn translucent, as these points are. `redundant_encoding` is zero
because nothing but colour tells the two treatments apart. Both rows pass once
shape is mapped as well, the darker vermillion is used as the second colour and
the points are drawn opaque:

```{r}
mended <- ggplot(crop_yield, aes(fertiliser, yield, colour = treatment,
                                 shape = treatment)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#005b96", "#d55e00")) +
  theme_depictr()

check_figure(mended)[, c("check", "measured", "threshold", "verdict")]
```

The vermillion need not be typed by hand.
`scale_colour_depictr(order = "contrast")` draws the groups in the
contrast-first order of `depictr_palette()`. It starts with the brand blue, the
vermillion and the reddish purple, the only three of the eight colours that
pass every colour row together. The bluish green comes fourth, and with it
four groups still keep 3:1 against white.
`depictr_options(palette = depictr_palette(order = "contrast"))` makes that
order the default for every later plot. Under that default, the second group
takes the vermillion, which depictr also uses as its accent for single
highlights.

The audit also takes a stated output width, because most figure text fails
unnoticed at its printed width. Text is drawn in points, so the text of a figure
saved seven inches wide and then printed in an 8.9 cm column is half the size
it was on screen:

```{r}
subset(check_figure(grouped, width_cm = 8.9), check == "text_size")
```

A figure saved at the size it will be printed is drawn at that size, so give
the saved width as both `width_cm` and `render_width_cm`, or leave both at
their defaults. `save_plot(check = TRUE)` runs the audit as it saves, at the
width it saves at, and warns about each check the figure fails.

Text drawn inside the panel, such as an annotation, a label or a cell value,
has a row of its own, `annotation_text_size`, held to the same floor as
`text_size`. That floor defaults to 6 pt, which is lenient. As their
guidelines stood on 30 September 2026, PLOS and APA Style asked for at least
8 pt, Elsevier for 7 pt and Nature for 5 to 7 pt, and `?check_figure` links
all four. Nature's range also has a ceiling, since no text but the panel
labels may exceed 7 pt. Passing `max_text_pt = 7` adds a row, `text_size_max`,
that holds a figure to that ceiling.

The eight-colour qualitative palette passes every colour-vision check and fails
the greyscale check. The Okabe-Ito guarantee covers hue confusion alone. The
palette's orange and sky blue differ by 0.79 in CIE lightness, so a
black-and-white printer renders them as the same grey. The greyscale check
holds the package's own palette to the same threshold as any other and reports
the measured difference. A figure that may be printed in black and white
should use fewer groups or a sequential palette, or add a redundant shape or
line type.

```{r}
eight <- data.frame(g = factor(letters[1:8]), x = 1:8, y = 1:8)
p8 <- ggplot(eight, aes(x, y, colour = g)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_colour_depictr() +
  theme_depictr()

subset(check_figure(p8), check == "greyscale_separability")
```

The audit does not measure a continuous colour or fill scale, such as that of
a heatmap. Its colour rows then report no result and give the reason. A ramp
is read by its lightness, so prefer one whose lightness changes evenly, such
as viridis or depictr's sequential and diverging ramps, over a rainbow
[@crameri2020].

Set the look once for a whole script with `depictr_options()`. It holds the
base size and family, the brand and accent colours and a custom palette. Called
with no arguments, it reports the current settings:

```{r}
depictr_options()
```

Supplying arguments sets them for every later plot and returns the previous
values, so you can put the look back afterwards:

```{r, fig.height = 4}
old <- depictr_options(base_size = 13, accent = "#b3589a")
coefficient_plot(fit, title = "Set once, applied everywhere")
do.call(depictr_options, old)   # restore the previous settings
```

## Where to next

The remaining articles go into each area in turn.
`vignette("exploring-data")` covers distributions, categories, bivariate plots,
scatter-plot matrices, correlations, missingness, outliers, summary tables and
the estimation plots.
`vignette("model-estimates")` covers forest plots, model comparison,
predicted values, interactions, random effects, optimiser checks and the
frequentist-over-Bayesian-posterior overlay.
`vignette("diagnostics-and-uncertainty")` covers residuals, GLM-appropriate
binned residuals, the classification suite (ROC, PR, gains, lift, calibration,
thresholds) on an imbalanced outcome, and power curves.
Two further articles, `vignette("multivariate-and-survival")` and
`vignette("time-series")`, cover the remaining methods.
